# The Hidden Costs of a "Cheap" Repair: A Washing Machine Story

When a household appliance breaks, the instinctive first question is often "how much will the part cost?" A quick search reveals that the drain pump for your washing machine costs only $25, and the temptation is to conclude that the repair should therefore be cheap and easy. This reasoning, however, misunderstands how modern appliance repair actually works. The price of a broken component is frequently the smallest factor in the total cost—financial and otherwise—of fixing a machine. Following a fictional washing machine through a realistic repair scenario illustrates why.

## The Diagnosis Problem

Our story begins when the machine, a five-year-old front-loader, refuses to spin and drains sluggishly. The owner correctly suspects the drain pump, but suspicion is not diagnosis. A washing machine that won't drain can be caused by a clogged drain hose, a jammed check valve, a foreign object lodged in the pump impeller, a failed pump motor, a faulty pressure switch that never tells the controller the tub is full, a broken wire harness, or even a software fault in the control board. Each of these possibilities points toward a different part, and some of them point toward no part at all.
